questions.q: What is the defining property of the imaginary unit i?
questions.explain: i is defined so that squaring it gives -1, which is the one new rule that makes the entire complex number system work -- no real number satisfies this.

questions.q: For the complex number 3 + 4i, what are the real part and imaginary part?
questions.explain: In a + bi form, a is the real part and b (not bi) is the imaginary part -- here a = 3 and b = 4.
Distributing gives 6 - 15i + 8i - 20i^2, and substituting i^2 = -1 turns -20i^2 into +20, giving (6+20) + (-15+8)i = 26 - 7i.

questions.q: A student multiplies two complex numbers and gets a final answer of 10 - 3i^2. What mistake did they make?
options: They forgot to substitute i^2 = -1 to finish simplifying the result
They used the wrong formula for addition instead of multiplication
Nothing is wrong -- this is a valid final answer
They should have gotten a negative real part
questions.explain: A fully simplified complex number should never contain i^2 (or any higher power of i) in the final answer -- it must always be replaced using i^2 = -1 and combined into the real part.

questions.q: Why does quantum computing require amplitudes to be complex numbers instead of just real numbers?
options: A complex number can encode both an amount and a phase relationship in a single coefficient, which a real number alone cannot represent
Complex numbers are simply a notational convenience with no real mathematical necessity
Qubits can only take integer values, and complex numbers are needed to represent integers
Real numbers cannot be added or multiplied, so complex numbers are required for arithmetic
questions.explain: A qubit amplitude needs to carry both 'how much' of a basis state and a phase that governs how states interfere -- a single real number can't hold both pieces, but a complex number can.
